div.p: With the emergence of multiprocessors, embedded systems are nowadays capable of handling diverse and complicated applications. Besides static workloads such as periodic tasks, dynamic workloads such as aperiodic tasks happen more frequently and become challenging to researchers to deal with. In this study, an effective scheduling approach for aperiodic tasks in multiprocessors is presented. An adaptive Local Assignment Algorithm with the integration of servers is introduced to schedule mixture systems of periodic and aperiodic tasks. Servers are dedicatedly preserved for aperiodic tasks at runtime. This scheduling scheme guarantees the schedulability of 100% without significantly increasing the time complexity. Simulation results show that the proposed mechanism effectively improves the responsiveness of aperiodic tasks while maintaining relatively low runtime overhead. In addition, it causes much fewer scheduler invocations in comparison with the existing algorithms.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent decades, multiprocessors have become dominant in embedded systems to support the increasingly diverse and complicated applications. Multiprocessors are introduced to increase the system capacity so that heavier task sets are adaptable. However, it is also faced with increase of computation complexity in the sense that the scheduler has to not only handle different types of tasks, but also manage multiple processing units. Scheduling hybrid task sets of periodic and aperiodic tasks with efficient exploitation of the system capacity is therefore important.

The problem of task scheduling on multiprocessors was first taken into account for periodic tasks, called periodic schedule, by Liu et. al [1]. A number of solutions for periodic schedule have been introduced. First simple solutions, which have low runtime overhead, are encountered by exploring well-known uniprocessor algorithms such as Earliest Deadline First (EDF) [2] on the context of multiprocessors. Typically, Global-EDF [3] applies EDF to schedule tasks in global scheduling scheme. EDF is also used to schedule subsets in partition scheduling scheme like partitioned-EDF [4] where task sets are separated into subsets each of which is served with a single processor. Disadvantage of these approaches is quite low schedulability [5]. Semi-partitioned scheduling was then introduced as a balance between the global and partitioned schedulings to improve the schedulability. The considerable candidate of this approach is semi-partitioned reservation [6] which achieved near-optimal scheduling with schedulability of 99.9%.

In trade-off with increase of time complexity, optimal algorithms are introduced, which can schedule any task sets of utilization of up to 100%. Pfair scheduling [8] was the very first solution which guarantees fairness for periodic tasks at every tick. Pfair, however, is faced with numerous scheduler invocations and dramatical increase of task preemption and migration due to the fragmentation of task executions. Alternatively, BF [9], LLREF [10], and DP-WRAP [11] achieved the optimality by guaranteeing the periodic schedule for intervals (or time periods). Interval-based schedulings have potential to reduce scheduler invocation. However, task preemption and migration are still problematic issues in LLREF while BF and DP-WRAP cause processors in idle times unnecessarily, which reduces the system performance. Later, RUN [12] emerged as an outperforming optimal approach in terms of task preemption and migration counts. Lastly, Local Assignment Algorithm (LAA) [13] was introduced as an optimal algorithm with relatively low time complexity. LAA exploits the intervalbased scheme to reduce the number of scheduling points and guarantees the system fully assigned on every interval to achieve the optimality. Full assignment on intervals allows LAA to better utilize the system capacity than BF and DP-WRAP since the unnecessary idle times of processors are reduced. In addition, LAA is free of off-line processing which is the strategy applied to reduce the runtime overhead in RUN.

Moreover, scheduling hybrid task sets is challenging to researchers since it often increases the runtime overhead due to unknown factors of the aperiodic tasks such as entering time and execution time. Aperiodic tasks can be scheduled in background with low scheduling cost when there exist processors unused by periodic tasks. This approach, however, produces long response times for aperiodic tasks. Effective online scheduling approaches are therefore expected to improve the aperiodic responsiveness. Contribution Characterized as low time complexity and unnecessity of off-line processing, LAA is likely promising to schedule hybrid task sets. In this paper, we present an adaptive Local Assignment Algorithm with integration of aperiodic servers to adapt to aperiodic tasks. The proposed algorithm is expected to schedule aperiodic tasks on-line together with periodic ones to shorten response times without significantly increasing time complexity.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II is specification of the targeted system with tasks' characteristics. Section III describes the procedure of the proposed scheduling algorithm with the integration of aperiodic servers. The schedulability of the system is then discussed in Section IV. Simulation environment and evaluation results come in Section V. Finally in Section VI is the conclusion.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: In this study, the targeted multiprocessor system is supposed to have m (m ≥ 2) identical processors. The system executes mixed task sets of periodic and aperiodic tasks. Tasks are all preemptable and independent of each other.

Let n p (n p ≥ 0) denote the number of periodic tasks. A periodic task τ i (0 ≤ i < n p ) is characterized by two parameters: a processor utilization µ i (µ i ≤ 1) and an integer period T i (T i > 0). The worst-case execution time of task τ i (C W CET i ) is then defined as:
div.formula: C W CET i = µ i * T i(1)
div.p: Periodic tasks are all supposed to have phase time equal to 0. Regularly, periodic tasks release jobs as their instant execution. Aperiodic tasks enter the system irregularly. All aperiodic tasks in the system are supposed to be soft ones; there is no deadline constraints on aperiodic tasks' completion. The aim of scheduling is to improve the aperiodic responsiveness while guaranteeing all periodic tasks to meet their deadlines. Our targeted system is restricted to feasible systems where np-1 i=0 µ i ≤ m.

div.head: III. ADAPTIVE LOCAL ASSIGNMENT ALGORITHM A. Integration of aperiodic servers
div.p: In order to schedule aperiodic tasks, we employ the concept of servers which are modeled equivalently to a periodic task with two parameters: utilization rate and period. Server utilizations are decided using the remaining system capacity unused by periodic tasks. Let U s denote the total utilization of servers, then U s = m -U p where U p is the total utilization of periodic tasks. U s is distributed to servers as their utilization as follows. There are U s servers with utilization of 1 and one server with utilization of U s -U s . If 0 < U p < m, then there are n s = U s + 1 servers established. This server establishment is similar to the concept of servers in [14].

Servers are supposed to have their periods arbitrarily large. The schedules of servers are preserved for aperiodic tasks' execution at runtime. The service of servers is decided in the following manner: Each server is assigned at most one aperiodic task for execution at a time and assignment of aperiodic tasks to servers greedily makes servers as busy as possible. Note that different aperiodic tasks are allowed to be executed concurrently on different servers. By this scheme, we convert the problem of scheduling aperiodic tasks to the problem of scheduling servers.

div.head: B. Definitions
div.p: In this paper, definitions of time interval, local requested execution time and fully-assigned system are basically inherited from the original LAA [13]. Differences are additional calculations in regard to aperiodic servers. Specifically, applying the notion of proportionate scheduling, local requested execution times of periodic tasks and servers on interval I = [t 1 , t 2 ) are calculated using Equation 2 and Equation 3 where A i (t 1 ) and As j (t 1 ) are the already-assigned resources of periodic tasks and servers up to t 1 (or on period [0, t 1 )), respectively.
div.formula: E i (t 1 , t 2 ) = µ i * t 2 -A i (t 1 )
Es j (t 1 , t 2 ) = U j * t 2 -As j (t 1 )(3)
div.p: Then, the fully-assigned system is guaranteed up to time t so that the total amount of already-assigned resources of periodic tasks and servers up to t is equal to the capacity of the system. That is,
div.formula: np-1 i=0 A i (t) + ns-1 j=0 As j (t) = m * t(4)

div.head: C. Scheduling algorithm
div.p: We extend the original LAA to the context of periodic tasks and servers. Algorithm 1 shows the procedure of the adaptive Local Assignment Algorithm (adaptive LAA) for making a scheduling plan for an interval. In this pseudo code, m denotes the number of processors. Periodic tasks and servers are indexed by i and j, respectively, where 0 ≤ i < n p and 0 ≤ j < n s . µ i and U j are the utilizations of periodic tasks and servers. JRE i is the remaining execution time of the current job of periodic task τ i , which is set to the task's WCET at the job release. Related to the interval, t s and t e (0 ≤ t s < t e ) indicate the start and end times of the involved interval and L I = t e -t s is the interval's length. The local requested execution times of periodic tasks and servers on the interval are expressed as E i (t s , t e ) and Es j (t s , t e ), respectively. A i (t s ) and As j (t s ) are the already-assigned resources of periodic tasks and servers up to t s . Finally, min() is function that finds the smallest value among input arguments.

The procedure of the adaptive LAA consists of three main steps. The first step, LRET Calculation, is to calculate the local requested execution times (LRETs) using Equation 2and Equation 3. This calculation determines the compulsory execution for periodic tasks and servers according to the proportionate scheduling. In the second step, LRET Adjustment, the LRETs are increased to exhaust the system capacity of the involved interval. In other words, this step guarantees the system fully assigned on the interval. To this end, the slack time (slack) obtained by subtracting LRETs of the first step from the capacity of the system is distributed to periodic tasks and servers appropriately. The distribution is designed as follows: (1) increasing LRETs of periodic tasks by unit amount with consideration of the remaining slack times, job's remaining execution time, and interval length; (2) increasing LRETs of servers by the smaller value between the remaining slack and the possible increment of the server on the interval defined by L I -Es j (t s , t e ); (3) distributing the left slack times to periodic tasks. When tasks and servers are given additional amounts, LRETs, job remaining execution times, and slack are updated with the amounts. Adding a unit amount to the LRETs of periodic tasks first is to guarantee for the tasks to satisfy their deadline constraints (similarly in [9]). The different way of increment applied to servers implies that servers prefer to increase their LRETs more than periodic tasks. This is aimed at improving the aperiodic responsiveness. The last step of distribution is to assure that all slots of the interval are fully utilized. In the final step, Task Arrangement, periodic tasks and servers are arranged on processors for their execution. A process consecutiveAssignment, which is described in detail in Algorithm 2, is proposed for this purpose. Basically, the idea of consecutive assignment in the original LAA is applied. That is, a virtual uniprocessor is established by concatenating actual processors together. Periodic tasks and servers are arranged on the virtual uniprocessor and then the obtained arrangement is converted to the execution order of tasks and servers on actual processors. In addition, we come up with a more complex procedure of the consecutive assignment (compared with [11]) with an attempt to improve the aperiodic responsiveness and reduce task preemption and migration.

As shown in Algorithm 2, input data of the assignment process include the number of processors (m), periodic task set (T asks), server set (Servers), and interval's length (L I ). Note that although excluded from the algorithm, LRETs obtained in the first two steps of Algorithm 1 are also used in this process. The output of the process is the expected scheduling plan for the interval, which is denoted as SP . Additionally, the process also utilizes past schedules on processors.

On each segment, allocation priority of periodic tasks is decided as follows: (1) task that has its LRET fitting the remaining space of the segment; (2) task that was executed on the next segment's processor at the slot just before the scheduling event; (3) task selected arbitrarily. In order to select the suitable task from the task set in the above priorities, three functions seekT askF it, seekT askLast, and seekT askRandom are implemented, respectively. The selected task tsk is then assigned to the current processor's segment p using function assignT ask. The task is allocated space continuously after the servers and tasks which have been already allocated on the same segment. The given space is equal to the task's LRET and may belong to two segments (p and p + 1). In this case the already assigned server on p + 1 is moved to give a fit space to the task. When segments take in task's requirement, their lengths are decreased by the amount.

Next, empty servers are continuously allocated to the remaining space on the segments using function assignEmptyServer. Assigning empty servers lastly has a meaning of preserving capacity for the coming aperiodic tasks and reducing unnecessary idle times of processors. Finally, the arrangement on the virtual uniprocessor is converted to the execution order of periodic tasks and servers on the actual processors corresponding to processors' segment. The conversion is done using function convertSchedule and SP is obtained as the expected scheduling plan for the interval.

div.head: D. Secondary scheduling event
div.p: In the scheduling scheme introduced above, the scheduling events are decided as the release times of (jobs of) periodic tasks. We call them primary scheduling events (primary invocation). In this section, we suggest to add secondary scheduling events (secondary invocation). A secondary scheduling event is decided as the time within an interval when an aperiodic task is released and there exists an empty server. At this time, the empty server is assigned the aperiodic task and becomes non-empty. The secondary scheduling event is introduced to reorder the non-empty servers' execution on the remaining span of the interval. Since the consecutive assignment in Algorithm 2 tends to assign non-empty servers ahead of periodic tasks on every processor, the reordering action has potential to improve the aperiodic responsiveness.

At the secondary invocation, step 3 of Algorithm 1, Task Arrangement, is the only process to make up the scheduling plans since the LRETs of periodic tasks and servers on the interval have been already obtained. The secondary invocations therefore add less runtime overhead than the primary ones although increasing the scheduler invocation.

div.head: Example of scheduling with secondary invocation
div.p: Figure 2 shows investigation of secondary invocation for the example in Figure 1. As the server is empty at the release time (time 6) of the aperiodic task, the scheduler is invoked as a secondary invocation. Figure 2(b) displays the scheduling plans which are made up at time 6. Since the non-empty server is arranged at the beginning of P 0, the aperiodic task can be executed immediately and then finished at time 8. The response time is therefore equal to 2, one slot shorter than that of the schedule without secondary invocation (Figure 2(a)).

div.head: IV. SCHEDULABILITY GUARANTEE
div.p: Since aperiodic servers are modeled like periodic tasks and the total utilization of periodic tasks and servers does not exceed the system capacity, it is possible to replace a server by a periodic task which has the same utilization and period as the server. By this way, proof of schedulability in Section III of [13] can be applied to show that the adaptive LAA can schedule any task sets of utilization of 100%. In other words, the adaptive LAA still maintains the optimality of the original LAA.

div.head: A. Simulation environment
div.p: The proposed algorithm is evaluated by simulation. The simulation environment is set up for cases of 4, 8, 16, and 32 identical processors. The observation period is 100,000 ticks. The utilization of periodic tasks is from 75% to 95% with increment of 5%. The maximum number of periodic tasks in a task set is 100. Periodic tasks' utilizations and periods are generated using exponential distribution. On the other hand, the utilization of aperiodic tasks is from 2% to 5%. The number of aperiodic releases in a task set is at least 3,000 during the observation period. For each scenario of the periodic task utilization and the number of processors, for example periodic utilization of 75% and 4 processors, all combinations of ten periodic task sets and twenty aperiodic task sets (totally 200 task sets) are simulated and the average result is exhibited. Due to limitations of space, only the results for 4 and 16 processors are shown. The other number of processors exhibited a similar trend.

The targeted criteria of the evaluation are responsiveness, time complexity, and scheduler invocation. Comparison candidates include the original LAA [13], Pfair [8], RUN [12], and semi-partition reservation (SPR) [6], [7]. Pfair is integrated with aperiodic servers [14] to schedule aperiodic tasks. On the other hand, aperiodic tasks are scheduled in background in the original LAA, RUN and SPR.

div.head: B. Simulation results
div.p: 1) Responsiveness: Figure 3 shows results of average response times of aperiodic tasks. LAA likely shows the worst results since it prioritizes periodic tasks to receive seamless executions ahead of aperiodic tasks on every interval. On the case of 4 processors, the adaptive LAA (ALAA) clearly shows the best results. However, when the number of processors increases, results of ALAA are overlapping with those of PFair and RUN although they are still better than SPR in almost cases. This is because the number of empty slots increases together with the number of processors and empty processors tend to arise more frequently. Exceptionally, at utilization of 95% on large number of processors, ALAA tends to be worse than RUN and SPR. The reason is that schedules of servers (and then the aperiodic tasks' execution) become fragmentary at heavy loads due to the proportionate calculation. 2) Time complexity: Time complexity is assessed through the maximum runtime overhead per tick. The runtime overhead of a scheduling algorithm is calculated by counting the number of clock cycles during which instructions in the algorithm are executed. The instruction set of the Cortex-A9 processor [15], [16] is referred to for this calculation. Runtime overheads caused by executing procedure to assign aperiodic tasks to servers when they are released are included in calculation of ALAA. the complex procedure of task classification, Pfair causes significantly higher runtime overhead than the other algorithms in our all cases of simulation. Therefore, it is not plotted in the figure. Overall, as a semi-partitioned scheduling, SPR shows the lowest runtime overhead. Except case of periodic utilizations of 80% and 85% on 4 processors, ALAA exhibits lower runtime overheads than RUN. Obviously, including servers the calculation of ALAA becomes more complexed than LAA, which results in higher runtime overhead. The results indicate that ALAA can achieve the optimality and improve the aperiodic responsiveness with a relatively low time complexity.

3) Scheduler invocation: Figure 5 displays results for the number of scheduler invocations. With introduction of secondary invocations, the adaptive LAA causes a bit larger number of scheduling points than the original LAA. Overall, LAA and ALAA outperform the other candidates in this criterion by over 50%. Combining with lower runtime overheads, fewer scheduler invocations also unveil efficiency of our solution in terms of improving the accumulative runtime overhead. This can improve the system performance since processors are preferably utilized for tasks' execution rather than executing the scheduling algorithm. In this paper, we presented an effective solution for the problem of scheduling mixture systems of periodic and aperiodic tasks on multiprocessors. Compared with the original algorithm, several modifications were introduced in adaptive Local Assignment Algorithm in order to improve the aperiodic responsiveness. By simulation, the proposed approach shows efficiency in enhancing the responsiveness of aperiodic tasks while guaranteeing relatively low time complexity in comparison with the existing algorithms. In addition, our algorithm issues significantly fewer scheduler invocations compared with the other candidates. The achieved results indicate that the adaptive Local Assignment Algorithm is positive to deal with dynamic workloads.

As shown in Algorithm 1, the local requested execution times of tasks and servers are calculated independently using their own parameters. In other words, it is possible for the local requested execution times to be calculated in parallel. A particular calculation mechanism is, therefore, expected to further reduce the runtime overhead.
